description: A team that surpasses the others
summary:
Ört (Kazakh for “fire”) is a web application that turns two decades of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar for Kazakhstan, from 2002 to today.

The problem: MODIS has observed fires since 2000, while VIIRS, its successor, detects three to five times more hotspots because of its finer 375 m resolution. Simply joining the records creates a false jump in fire activity after 2012. In our data, naive stitching suggests fires rose by 77%, while the harmonized series shows they actually fell by 55%.

We cleaned 3.1 million FIRMS detections, removing gas flares, low-confidence points and duplicates, aggregated them into 1 km fire cell-days, and calibrated VIIRS to the MODIS scale for each region using the 2012–2019 overlap period. We compared a ratio method with a machine-learning model, validated both on years they never saw, and reduced the error roughly fifteenfold compared with raw data.

The site shows a year-by-month heatmap calendar, a map, typical fire seasons and anomalous months for all 17 regions and 3 cities, with uncertainty ranges.

Emergency services, scientists and land managers can finally see when and where burning truly happens, and prepare for critical periods.
details:
What it does

Ört (Kazakh for “fire”) is a web application that shows a harmonized burning activity calendar for Kazakhstan from July 2002 to October 2026. It merges fire detections from two NASA satellite instruments, MODIS and VIIRS, into a single consistent time series. As a result, the instrument a detection came from no longer matters, and users can focus on real seasonal patterns, trends and anomalies.

The problem we solve

MODIS (about 1 km pixels) has recorded fires since 2000. VIIRS (375 m pixels), its successor, has done so since 2012. VIIRS detects three to five times more hotspots, so simply switching from one record to the other creates a false surge in fire activity after 2012. In our data, naive stitching suggests a 77% increase after 2012, while the harmonized record shows a 55% decrease. Without harmonization, fire managers would draw the wrong conclusions.

How it works

1. Data. We downloaded 40 yearly archives from NASA FIRMS (Archive Download, country: Kazakhstan, 5 km buffer): MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m Collection 2, standard science-quality data plus near-real-time data for the latest months. Regional boundaries for all 17 regions, including Abai, Jetisu and Ulytau created in 2022, and the 3 major cities come from OpenStreetMap via Overpass.

2. Cleaning. From 3.1 million raw detections we removed duplicates, Terra MODIS (keeping only Aqua, whose afternoon overpass matches VIIRS and avoids a second artificial jump in 2002), static heat sources such as gas flares and offshore platforms, and low-confidence points. Near-real-time data has no source-type field, so we built a mask of persistent industrial hotspots from historical data and applied it there. Finally, we clipped all points to official region polygons. This left 537,000 MODIS and 1.42 million VIIRS detections.

3. Aggregation. Points are aggregated into fire cell-days on a roughly 1 km grid: several detections in the same cell on the same day count as one fire signal, which removes VIIRS’s multiple-pixel duplication.

4. Harmonization. During the 2012–2019 overlap, when both sensors flew, we learned how VIIRS relates to MODIS in each region. We compared three approaches: raw VIIRS, a regional ratio calibration, and a LightGBM machine-learning model that uses VIIRS counts, fire radiative power, season, region and day/night share. Each method was tested with leave-one-year-out validation on 2012–2019 and on a separate 2020–2025 holdout. The selection rule was fixed in advance: the method with the lowest error in leave-one-year-out validation is used. The regional ratio won by a small margin (mean error 14.8 vs 15.1 fire cell-days per region-month), while LightGBM performed better on 2020–2025 (9.3 vs 10.9). Both reduced the error about fifteenfold compared with raw VIIRS (221.1). Every harmonized value comes with an uncertainty range based on how the ratio varies between years.

5. Analytics. Typical seasons (median and 10th–90th percentile band over 2003–2025), anomalous months (robust z-scores on log-transformed counts), peak months and year-versus-normal indicators for every region.

The web application

A year-by-month heatmap calendar with Raw MODIS / Raw VIIRS / Harmonized views, a regional map with monthly hotspots, a sensor comparison chart that shows the 2012 jump disappearing, typical-season and anomaly views, and a Method page explaining our approach and its limitations. The interface is available in English, Russian and Kazakh and works on phones.

Tools and technologies

- Data processing: Python, pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, LightGBM, Matplotlib, Kaggle Notebooks (cloud CPU/GPU)

- Data sources: NASA Earthdata FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP C2), OpenStreetMap boundaries

- Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Apache ECharts, MapLibre GL JS with OpenFreeMap, react-i18next, Zustand, zod for data validation

- Collaboration and hosting: Git, GitHub, Vercel

- Hardware: team laptops and Kaggle cloud computing

- AI use: AI assistants (Claude, Claude Code) helped with research, code generation and documentation. All data decisions and results were reviewed by the team.

What makes it creative

- We treat a cloudy or missing day as “no data”, never as “no fire”.

- We keep raw and harmonized series side by side, so users can see the correction instead of trusting a black box.

- We avoided hidden artificial jumps by using a single satellite per sensor (Aqua, S-NPP).

- We built a flare mask so near-real-time data stays clean.

- The fire color ramp increases in brightness, so it is readable with color-vision deficiency.

Factors we considered

Scientific validity (validation on unseen years, uncertainty bands), accessibility (colorblind-safe palette, keyboard navigation, three languages), honesty about limitations (cloud cover is not modeled; preliminary near-real-time months are labeled), and scalability: the same pipeline works for any country by downloading its FIRMS archive.

Intended impact

Kazakhstan’s steppe faces recurring spring and late-summer fires from stubble burning and dry grassland. Ört gives emergency services, early warning teams, scientists and land managers a trustworthy picture of when and where burning truly happens, so they can plan resources before critical periods and quickly spot unusual months.
